newsitem.title: USA: Interim nuclear dump bill chances dim-Nevada sen..
newsitem.headline: Interim nuclear dump bill chances dim-Nevada sen..

text.p: Opponents of a bill to build a temporary dump in Nevada for radioactive wastes from nuclear power plants said they were confident the legislation would be be blocked.
"We've been assured many times by the administration that President Clinton will veto the bill, and we will have the votes to sustain the veto," an aide to Nevada Sen. Harry Reid said.

Reid and Richard Bryan, the state's two Democratic senators, oppose a bill being pushed by Republican Sens. Frank Murkowski of Alaska, who chairs the Senate Energy Committee, and Larry Craig of Idado to build a temporary nuclear waste dump in Nevada.
"Those senators are westerners and should know not to count their chickens before the eggs are hatched," an Energy Committee Republican aide said of Nevada's senators.
"It would be premature and irresponsible to claim victory before senators have even marked up the bill," the aide said.

Murkowski scheduled a committee vote for Wednesday on his bill that died last year under Clinton's veto threat. The committee aide said amendments were expected to be offered that could change votes when the bill reaches the full Senate.
The Senate last July voted 63-37 to pass the bill, but that was short of the 67 votes needed to override Clinton's promised veto. Because of that, the House did not move on a companion bill.

"I think it's going to be similar to last year's outcome. They needed four more. I don't think that they're there, and most other folks I've talked to all seem to think that we'll be able to sustain a veto," Bill Magavern, of Public Citizen's Critical Mass Project, said.

But Steve Unglesbee, of the Nuclear Energy Institute which supports the bill, said the issue has more urgency this year with the approaching January 31, 1998, deadline for the federal government to take control of the waste.
Unglesbee said 52 supporters of the bill returned to the Senate this year. "That's where we're starting from. We've got some work to do, obviously, but we're not starting from scratch," he said.
Under a 1982 law, the federal government next year is to take control of nuclear waste now being stored at some 70 sites across the country.

The administration is evaluating putting a permanent waste dump in Yucca Mountain in Nevada, but opposes the interim storage bill because it says it would divert resources from building the permanent facility and would prejudge Nevada as the ultimate dump site.

But the nuclear power industry said the permanent storage facility will not be completed before 2010 at the earliest, and said the government is obligated to take the waste off the industry's hands next year.
Utilities have paid some $12 billion into a fund to finance the federal disposal program.
